current_episode.title: The GCC Energy Outlook with Carmen Hamze

guest.bio_context: Carmen Hamze has been working in the energy sector for over 14 years across the GCC. She studied biology and initially pursued a career in biomedical research and healthcare consulting before transitioning into energy consulting at a GCC utility, where she remained and built her expertise in energy strategy and sustainability.

context.transcript_excerpt: Everyone was talking about net zero, the environment, let's get rid of hydrocarbons, etc. And what I've come to realize in the last 10 years working in the energy sector, that there's not one solution that's going to solve everything, it's multiple. Nuclear will still be part of the mix somewhere. We still need gas, data centers, they will require a lot of energy. This is what could potentially create one of the biggest energy hubs in the world. Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the second episode of Beyond the Deck here at Rollenberger. This is the podcast where we jump out of the PowerPoint decks and into the stories that are shaping in the region and, of course, also the world. Today, we're going to be focusing on the energy sector here across the GCC. And with me, I have an esteemed colleague, Carmen Hamze, who's been working on the energy sector for over 14 years across the GCC. And she's a partner here with us in Rollenberger. So, first of all, a warm welcome to the podcast, Carmen. Thank you, Dorival. It's good to be here and I hope we will have an insightful conversation. Great, great. We'll make it nice and energetic. So, just to get us started, Carmen, if you could just give us a little bit of what the current landscape is of the energy sector here across the GCC. It's a good question. I would say it's exciting times to be working and engaging in the energy sector in the GCC. If I want to take a look back or look at the outlook, I would summarize it in three aspects. One, there's a shift from previously being focusing on siloed energy subsectors like oil and gas, and now it's more about a portfolio approach. So, meaning we're looking at AI and the impact of, let's say, data centers and the need for renewable energy. Two, looking at gas as the backbone because you're going to have renewable energy going in. Then you have low carbon molecules like low LNG, hydrogen, CCUS. And then you have the traditional oil and gas, which now the shift is more towards sustainable energy. But it's a balance, thinking about it based on the trilemma, sustainability, energy security, and affordability. So, that's what guides the approach. And as you can see, if you look back five years ago, everyone was talking about net zero, the environment, let's get rid of hydrocarbons, etc. The GCC took a balanced approach. And I think now everyone's taking the same approach, and they are ahead in the thinking. They think about sustainable energy. You need to capture the carbon. But at the same time, we need to make sure we have secure sources of energy. You need to have reliable energy. So, those are all different aspects that are shaping the energy sector in the GCC. Excellent. Well, thanks. There's a lot to unpack there, right? And I really like what you mentioned regarding this portfolio approach, taking more of an integrated, from multiple sources, right? But you also mentioned some things that are on the demand side, like the data centers, and some things on the supply side, like renewable energy generation, etc. Of all these trends, which ones do you see as being the most, let's say, immediate, right? Because I've been hearing about green hydrogen, for example, for a while. Andrew Forrest, for example, out of Australia, was really driving this five years ago. Now it's kind of – I feel at least there's some loss of momentum in green hydrogen. Tell me a little bit about what are the immediate breakthroughs that we're going to see that are really going to drive the next five years or something? I'm still of a believer that it's still going to be there. But before, they were assuming it's going to be the solution to all. pending_qa.q: What role can smart meters and digitalization play in improving energy efficiency?
pending_qa.r: Smart meters provide real-time data on customer consumption, enabling more accurate billing and allowing consumers to see their usage patterns. This drives behavior-driven efficiency solutions and enables retail operators to offer energy-saving recommendations. The data can also be monetized to understand consumer behavior patterns, and digital tools enable predictive maintenance and grid modernization through IoT and sensors.

pending_qa.q: What skills and educational background are needed for careers in the modernized energy sector?
pending_qa.r: Beyond traditional engineering roles, the sector now requires foundational expertise in AI, data science, and understanding of the energy ecosystem. However, transferable skills are equally important—systemic thinking, adaptability, and the ability to evolve with changing technology are critical. A non-traditional background like biology can be valuable if combined with solid foundational knowledge and an agile mindset.

pending_qa.q: What is the long-term energy mix outlook for the GCC beyond five years?
pending_qa.r: The future energy mix will include all available solutions: nuclear will remain part of the mix, low-carbon molecules will play a massive role, renewable energy will continue growing as costs decline, LNG will remain crucial in the next five years, and digital and AI will permeate operations, decision-making, and tariff-setting. Private sector participation will also increase significantly in the region's energy sector.

pending_qa.q: How will electric vehicles adoption develop in the GCC over the next five years?
pending_qa.r: The GCC will adopt a balanced approach rather than moving to 100 percent electric vehicles. The region will see hybrid adoption, with some trucks and vehicles transitioning to electric or hydrogen, while traditional internal combustion engine vehicles will continue. The strategy is to adopt whatever works best rather than abandoning technologies that are already performing well.

pending_qa.q: Why is localizing solar and wind component manufacturing important for the GCC energy sector?
pending_qa.r: Localizing manufacturing of solar and wind components will have massive impacts on job creation, GDP growth, and localization scores. It also positions the region as a hub for import-export and enables it to provide clean energy not only within the GCC but beyond, while the CBAM carbon border adjustment mechanism makes clean power production an attraction factor for industrial players.
